title: How to organise a small Shopify warehouse
titleEs: Cómo organizar una bodega pequeña de Shopify
brief: Somebody with a spare room or a unit, boxes on the floor, and no system. What to name shelves, how granular to go, and when bins start paying off.
briefEs: Alguien con un cuarto libre o una bodega alquilada, cajas en el piso y ningún sistema. Cómo nombrar los estantes, qué tan detallado ir, y cuándo los bins empiezan a pagarse solos.
body:
Most small warehouses don't start as warehouses. They start as a spare room, then a garage, then a rented unit, and somewhere in that growth the "system" quietly disappears. You still remember where things are because you put them there yourself. The trouble starts when you can't remember anymore, or when someone else has to find something and can't.

Here's how to put a basic structure in place before it becomes urgent.

Start with zones, not bins

Before you label a single shelf, walk the space and divide it into zones. This can be as simple as "front wall," "middle racking," "overflow corner." Zones exist so that when you're looking for something, you're searching a section, not the whole room. If your unit has any natural divisions — aisles, rooms, a mezzanine — use those as your first layer.

Don't overthink this step. Four or five zones is plenty for a small operation. You're not designing an airport, you're giving yourself a starting point.

Naming shelves and racks: boring is correct

Resist the urge to name locations after what's currently stored there — "candles shelf," "the winter stuff rack." Stock moves. Names should describe the location, not the contents. A simple code works better than it sounds like it should:

  • A1, A2, A3 for zone A, shelf 1, 2, 3
  • B-R2-S3 for zone B, rack 2, shelf 3
  • Row-and-column codes if your shelving is laid out in a grid

The exact scheme matters less than consistency. Pick one pattern and use it everywhere, including on new shelving you add later. A mix of naming styles is worse than a bad naming style, because it means everyone has to remember which system applies where.

How granular to go

This is where people either overdo it or underdo it. Too broad ("Zone A") and you still have to hunt through a whole shelf's worth of boxes to find one SKU. Too granular ("Zone A, Shelf 2, Bin 4, Left Side, Second Row") and nobody will maintain it, including you.

A reasonable rule: go granular enough that one location holds one product, or a small enough number of products that you can eyeball the right one in a few seconds. If a shelf holds forty different SKUs, that's not a location, that's a pile with a label on it.

For small warehouses, this usually means individual bins or boxes within a shelf, each with their own code, rather than treating the whole shelf as one address. It costs a bit more time upfront. It saves that time back every single day someone has to fulfil an order.

When boxes-on-the-floor stops working

There's no shame in boxes on the floor when you're small. The problem isn't the boxes — it's the moment your memory stops being a reliable index of where everything is. A few signs that moment has arrived:

  • You or an employee spend real time each day searching for stock that should take seconds to find
  • New hires can't locate products without someone walking them there personally
  • You've shipped the wrong variant because two similar products were near each other with no distinction
  • A cycle count turns into a half-day event because nothing has a fixed home

None of these are catastrophic on their own. But they compound. Time spent searching is time not spent packing, and it's the kind of cost that's easy to ignore because it doesn't show up as a line item anywhere.

Where bins start paying for themselves

Once you've got zones, shelf codes, and a decision about how granular to go, you technically have a location system already — on paper, or in your head, or scrawled on a whiteboard. That's genuinely enough for some operations. If you've got a small enough catalog and a good memory, don't let anyone tell you that you need software to run a spare room.

The point where it's worth formalising is usually when more than one person needs to know where things are, or when your SKU count has grown past what any one person can hold in their head, or when receiving new stock means someone has to guess where it goes because the old system was never written down properly.

That's the point where Bins-USA tends to make sense for Shopify sellers — it takes the shelf and bin codes you've already worked out and ties them to your actual product records, so anyone doing picking, receiving, or a cycle count can scan a location instead of asking around. It's not a replacement for a sensible layout. It's what keeps a sensible layout from decaying once more than one person is relying on it.

Get the naming and granularity right first. The system you build on paper is the same one you'll eventually put into software, so it's worth getting it right while it still only costs you an afternoon.

title: Bin naming that still makes sense at 400 bins
titleEs: Nombres de bins que siguen teniendo sentido con 400 bins
brief: Aisle-rack-shelf schemes, why sequential numbers fall apart, and how to leave room to grow.
briefEs: Esquemas de pasillo-rack-estante, por qué la numeración secuencial se cae, y cómo dejar espacio para crecer.
body:
Most warehouses start with something simple: box 1, box 2, box 3. It works fine for the first month. Then you add a rack, then another aisle, and someone asks "where's box 47?" and the answer is a long pause. By the time you hit a few hundred bins, a naming scheme that isn't built to scale turns into a daily tax on everyone who picks, packs, or receives.

The good news is that fixing this doesn't require new shelving or a big project. It requires a naming convention that describes location, not history.

Why sequential numbers fall apart

Sequential numbering (bin 1 through bin 400) feels easy at first because it matches the order you built things in. The problem is it encodes nothing about where a bin actually is. Bin 212 could be next to bin 213 or on the other side of the building, depending on when you added it. New hires can't guess locations from the number. Nobody can look at a pick list and mentally route a path through the warehouse, because the numbers don't correspond to physical layout.

It also breaks the moment you rearrange anything. Add a rack in the middle of an aisle and you either renumber everything downstream or you create an ugly gap that nobody remembers the reason for. Six months later someone finds bin "212B" wedged in between 212 and 213 and has no idea why it isn't just 213.

A scheme that describes location

The fix almost every warehouse eventually lands on is some version of aisle-rack-shelf-position: a code that tells you where the bin is just by reading it, no lookup required.

  • Aisle — a letter or number for each physical aisle (A, B, C or 01, 02, 03).
  • Rack or bay — which rack within that aisle, numbered in a consistent direction (always left to right facing the aisle, for example).
  • Shelf or level — vertical position, usually numbered bottom to top or top to bottom, pick one and stay consistent.
  • Position — if a shelf holds multiple bins side by side, a final letter or number for left-to-right position.

So a bin named A-03-02-C tells a trained employee: aisle A, third rack, second shelf, position C. No memorization needed. Someone who has been on the floor for a week can walk straight to it, and someone who has never seen your warehouse can find it faster than someone reading off a bin numbered 1,842.

This also makes pick lists genuinely useful. If your list is sorted by bin location, and the bin names reflect physical layout, the picker walks a logical path through the building instead of zigzagging based on numeric order that has nothing to do with geography.

Leave room to grow

The single biggest mistake in bin naming isn't the format — it's not leaving gaps. If you number shelves 1, 2, 3, 4 with nothing in between, you can never insert a shelf without renaming everything above it. Number in increments instead: 10, 20, 30, 40. Now if you add a shelf between the first two, it becomes 15, and nothing else has to change.

The same logic applies to aisles and racks. If you have six aisles today, don't assume you'll never add a seventh in the middle of the building because of a layout change. Leaving letter or number gaps costs nothing now and saves a full relabeling project later.

Also decide early how you'll name overflow or temporary locations — receiving staging, a returns cart, a pallet that doesn't fit its normal bin. If these don't have a naming pattern, they become invisible: nobody records them because there's no obvious name to give them, and inventory quietly goes untracked in the gaps.

Keep it human-readable, not just database-friendly

It's tempting to design a scheme that's clever for a spreadsheet but useless out loud. If nobody can say a bin name to a coworker across the warehouse without spelling it out, it's too complex. Keep the pattern short, keep the delimiters consistent (always hyphens, always the same number of digits), and avoid characters that get confused when read aloud or scanned — skip the letter O and the number 0 together, skip I and 1.

If you're printing labels for scanning, this matters even more, since a barcode scan removes ambiguity but a human still has to read the label to know they're standing at the right bin before they scan it.

Where this gets easier with software

A consistent naming scheme is something you can plan on paper or a spreadsheet, and plenty of small warehouses run this way for a while. Where it gets harder is keeping it accurate as bins fill, empty, split, and multiply — and making sure everyone on the floor is looking at the same location data instead of a printout from three weeks ago.

That's the part Bins-USA is built for: bins tied to actual inventory counts, scanning to confirm someone's at the right location, and pick lists that follow your real layout instead of an arbitrary list order. The naming scheme is still yours to design — the app just keeps it enforced and current instead of something written on a whiteboard that goes stale.

Get the naming right first, on paper if you have to. Everything else — scanning, counts, pick routes — works better once the bins themselves make sense.

title: Five things that slow down picking
titleEs: Cinco cosas que hacen lenta la selección
brief: Walking order, one product in several bins, no barcode, batching, and printing the list too late.
briefEs: El orden de recorrido, un producto en varios bins, sin código de barras, el trabajo por lotes, e imprimir la lista demasiado pronto.
body:
Picking feels like it should be simple: get the order, walk to the product, put it in a box. But if picking is slow in your warehouse, it's almost never because your pickers are slow. It's because the layout, the paperwork, or the process is working against them. Here are five things that quietly add minutes to every pick, and what to do about each one.

Walking order that ignores the warehouse layout

Most pick lists are generated in the order items were added to the cart, or alphabetically by SKU, or in whatever order the system feels like that day. None of those match how your warehouse is laid out. A picker ends up walking to aisle 3, then back to aisle 1, then over to aisle 9, then back to aisle 2 — covering the same ground three or four times on a single order.

The fix isn't complicated: sort the pick list by bin location, not by SKU or order sequence. If your bins are numbered in a logical path through the warehouse, a list sorted that way turns a zigzag into a straight walk. This is one of the more useful things a bin system can do for you — once every product has a real location on file, the list can follow the floor instead of the spreadsheet.

One product living in several bins at once

This happens more than people admit. A product gets restocked and there's no room in its usual spot, so a second batch goes on a shelf two aisles over. Nobody writes it down. Now that SKU exists in two places, but only one of them is in anyone's head — usually the head of whoever put it there.

When a new picker gets that order, they go to the one location they know, find it empty or short, and either guess, ask around, or walk the whole warehouse hunting for the rest of the stock. Multiply that by a few SKUs a day and it adds up to real time lost.

The only real fix is recording every bin a product lives in, not just the "main" one, so the pick list can point to all of them. This is exactly the kind of thing that falls apart with sticky notes and shelf labels, and exactly the kind of thing Bins-USA tracks by design — a product can have more than one bin, and the pick list knows about all of them.

No barcode, so everything is visual matching

If bins and products aren't barcoded, picking turns into a matching game: read the SKU on the list, read the label on the shelf, compare them character by character, hope you didn't misread a 0 for an O. It's slow even when it works, and when it doesn't work, you ship the wrong item and someone finds out three days later.

Barcodes on bins and products turn that comparison into a scan. It's faster, and it removes the specific kind of error that comes from tired eyes reading similar-looking SKUs at 4pm. If you're doing any volume at all, this is one of the cheaper fixes on this list relative to what it saves.

Picking one order at a time instead of batching

If your warehouse gets ten small orders in an hour and a picker walks each one separately, that's ten trips down the same aisles, often passing the same shelves five or six times. Batching — grouping orders that share products or nearby locations and picking them together — cuts that walking dramatically. It takes a bit more organization on the front end (separating items back into their individual orders after picking), but for anyone shipping multiple orders a day, the walking time saved usually outweighs the sorting time added.

Batching doesn't need to be complicated. Even a simple rule — "combine any orders that share three or more SKUs" — catches a lot of the easy wins without turning your process into a puzzle.

Printing the pick list before the order is actually settled

This one's less about the warehouse floor and more about timing. If pick lists print the moment an order comes in, before payment fully clears, before an address issue gets flagged, before a customer adds a second item five minutes later — you end up picking orders that change, get canceled, or need to be reprinted with an addition. The picker does the walk twice for one order.

Building in a short buffer before printing, or triggering the print from a status change rather than order creation, avoids most of this. It won't catch everything, but it stops the most common version of the problem: picking, then immediately re-picking.

None of these fixes require ripping up your process. Most of them are about making the information a picker needs — location, quantity, barcode, batch — available at the moment they need it, instead of making them carry it in their head or figure it out on the fly.

title: Cycle counting without closing for a day
titleEs: Conteo cíclico sin cerrar un día entero
brief: Counting a few bins a week instead of everything at once, which bins to start with, and what to do with the differences.
briefEs: Contar unos pocos bins por semana en vez de todo de golpe, por cuáles bins empezar, y qué hacer con las diferencias.
body:
Full physical inventory counts are miserable. You shut the warehouse down, pull everyone off picking and receiving, and spend a day or two counting things that were probably fine to begin with. Then three weeks later the counts are already drifting again because nobody's checking anything in between. Cycle counting is the alternative: you count a small number of bins on a regular schedule, all year, and you never have to close the doors.

Count a few bins, not the whole warehouse

The idea is simple. Instead of one huge count once or twice a year, you break the warehouse into pieces and count a piece at a time — a handful of bins a day, or a section a week, whatever fits your staffing. Nobody stops working. A picker or a receiving clerk with fifteen free minutes can knock out a few bins between other tasks.

Over a few months, every bin in the building gets counted at least once, usually more than once for the busy ones. You catch errors close to when they happened instead of finding them eleven months later with no idea how they got there. And because you're only touching a small area at a time, a count that turns up a problem doesn't derail your whole day — you fix it and move on.

This only works if you actually stick to a schedule. "We'll get to it when things slow down" means it never happens. Put it on the calendar like any other recurring task — pick two bins every morning before the first pick wave, or one aisle every Friday afternoon.

Which bins to start with

Don't just start at aisle one and work across. Prioritize:

  • High-velocity bins first. The SKUs that move every day are the ones where a wrong count actually costs you — a stockout, an oversell, a picker standing in front of an empty bin. Count these most often.
  • Bins with a history of problems. If a location has been wrong before, or the product there gets picked and repacked constantly, count it more often than a slow-moving shelf in the back.
  • High-value items. Even if they don't move fast, a bin holding expensive product is worth checking regularly — the dollar impact of being wrong is bigger.
  • Anything that had a recent transfer, return, or receiving exception. Movement is where errors get introduced. A bin that just had product moved into or out of it is a good candidate for a near-term recount.
  • Random sampling for everything else. For slow movers and low-value stock, a rotating random pick is fine — you just want to make sure nothing goes untouched for a year straight.

A simple ABC split works for most warehouses: A items (your top movers) get counted monthly, B items quarterly, C items once or twice a year. You don't need software to do this — a spreadsheet with a count date column works, though if you're tracking bins in Bins-USA, cycle counts and the count history are already tied to the same bin and location records you use for picking, so you're not maintaining a separate list.

What to do when the count doesn't match

You will find differences. That's the point of counting — finding them while they're small and recent instead of large and mysterious. When a bin count doesn't match what the system says, don't just overwrite the number and move on. A few steps first:

  • Recount before you adjust anything. A lot of "discrepancies" are just miscounts — someone misread a label, counted a partial case as a full one, or missed a unit tucked behind something. A second look by a different person catches this fast.
  • Check for an unrecorded transaction. Look at recent receiving, transfers, and picks for that bin. Often the missing units show up in a nearby bin, or there's an order that shipped without the pick being logged, or a transfer that was physically done but never entered.
  • Note the cause, not just the number. If you can tell why it happened — mislabeled bin, wrong item put away, a return dumped in the wrong spot — write that down. A running log of causes tells you where your actual process is breaking, not just that your inventory is "off."
  • Adjust and move on. Once you're confident in the recount, update the system to match reality and note the date. Don't leave a known-wrong number sitting in the system waiting for the next full count to fix it.
  • Watch for repeat offenders. If the same bin is wrong two cycles in a row, something about that location is the problem — bad labeling, awkward layout, two SKUs that look alike sitting next to each other. Fix the location, not just the count.

This is where scanning helps more than a clipboard: a barcode scan confirms you're counting the bin and item you think you're counting, and it timestamps the count automatically so you're not relying on someone's memory of when they checked it.

None of this requires a big rollout. Pick five bins this week, count them, write down what you find, and do five more next week. In a few months you'll have a warehouse where the numbers on the screen actually match what's on the shelf — without ever losing a full day to find out.

title: Shopify locations are not bins
titleEs: Las ubicaciones de Shopify no son bins
brief: What Shopify tracks, what it does not, and why quantity without position is only half an inventory.
briefEs: Qué rastrea Shopify, qué no, y por qué la cantidad sin la posición es media respuesta.
body:
Shopify's Locations feature tells you how much of a product you have and which building it's in. That's useful. If you run one warehouse or a warehouse plus a storefront, Locations answers "do we have it, and where in the world is it." It does not answer "where in the building is it." Those are two different questions, and only one of them gets a picker to the product in under a minute.

What Shopify actually tracks

A Shopify location is a big, coarse container: a warehouse, a store, a 3PL. Inventory quantities are tied to that location. You can see that 340 units of a SKU sit at "Main Warehouse." You cannot see, inside Shopify, that 200 of those units are on Rack A, shelf 3, and the other 140 are in a bin near receiving because nobody had time to consolidate them last Tuesday. Shopify was not built to go below the building level, and it doesn't pretend to. That's not a criticism of the platform — it's just the edge of what the feature is for.

Why quantity without position is half an answer

Think about what actually happens when an order comes in. Someone has to physically walk to the product and pick it. If your system tells you the quantity but not the position, that walk becomes a search: check the usual spot, ask around, check the overflow shelf, check if it got moved during the last reorganization. Multiply that by every order, every day, every new hire who doesn't have the layout memorized yet. Quantity tells you the order can be fulfilled in theory. Position is what makes it happen in practice.

This gap is invisible when a warehouse is small enough that one or two people carry the whole layout in their heads. It becomes very visible the moment you add a second person, a second shift, or enough SKUs that nobody's memory is reliable anymore. At that point, "we know where things are" quietly turns into "Dave knows where things are," which is a staffing risk, not an inventory system.

The signs you've outgrown memory-based storage

  • New employees take weeks to get fast at picking, because the layout isn't written down anywhere they can check it.
  • The same SKU ends up in two or three different spots because whoever put stock away didn't know where the existing stock was.
  • Cycle counts take longer than they should because counting means searching first, counting second.
  • Nobody wants to take a vacation during a busy stretch, because the internal map of the warehouse leaves with them.
  • You've started keeping a spreadsheet of "where things are" next to Shopify, and it's already out of date.

If two or more of these sound familiar, the problem isn't your product count or your order volume — it's that you have inventory data and location data living in two different places, one of them being nowhere formal at all.

What a bin actually adds

A bin is just a named, specific spot — a shelf, a box, a section of a rack — that a SKU is assigned to and that stays associated with it in your system. Once that assignment exists, "where is it" stops being a question anyone has to answer from memory. A pick list can tell a picker to go to Bin C-14 instead of just naming the product and letting them figure out the rest. A receiving worker can put stock away and record the bin at the same time, instead of putting it wherever there's space and hoping someone remembers. A cycle count can be done bin by bin instead of hunting SKU by SKU.

This is the layer Shopify doesn't have, and it's the layer that matters once you're managing real physical space with real people walking around in it. Bins-USA sits on top of Shopify to add exactly this: bin assignments, scanning, and pick lists that reference actual shelf locations, not just the warehouse as a whole. It doesn't change what Shopify tracks at the location level — it fills in what happens once you're inside that location.

You don't need a system to start

You can get most of the benefit with a notebook and some labels, if you're disciplined about it. Assign every product a specific spot. Write it down somewhere everyone can check. Update it the moment something moves, not "later." The value isn't in the software — it's in the discipline of always knowing where something lives instead of always having to look. Software just makes that discipline easier to keep once your SKU count or headcount makes a notebook unreliable.

Shopify will always tell you what you have. Whether you also know exactly where it sits is a separate problem, and it's worth solving on its own terms — with a spreadsheet, a label maker, or a system built for it.

title: Receiving a pallet without losing an afternoon
titleEs: Recibir un pallet sin perder la tarde
brief: Scanning into a bin as you unload, when to label, and why the fast path is one bin at a time.
briefEs: Escanear a un bin mientras descarga, cuándo etiquetar, y por qué el camino rápido es un bin a la vez.
body:
A pallet shows up, the driver wants a signature, and you've got a stack of boxes that need to become inventory in your system before anyone can sell them. It's tempting to unload the whole thing first, stack it in the aisle, and deal with the counting later. That's usually how an afternoon disappears.

Unload and log at the same time

The fastest receiving process doesn't separate "get it off the truck" from "get it into the system." Every box you touch, you touch once. Pull it off the pallet, scan it, put it in its bin, move to the next box. If you set the pallet down and plan to come back to the scanning later, you'll end up recounting things, guessing which box was which, and cross-checking against a packing slip that's already covered in coffee rings.

This matters more with mixed pallets than single-SKU ones. A pallet of one product is easy to eyeball later. A pallet with a case of one item, half a case of another, and a handful of loose units of a third is exactly where mistakes happen if you're relying on memory instead of scanning as you go.

One bin at a time, not one product at a time

It's natural to think "let me get all the widgets put away, then all the gadgets." In practice, that means walking back and forth across the warehouse multiple times, and holding partial counts in your head between trips. The faster path is the opposite: pick a bin, put away everything that belongs there from this delivery, confirm the count, then move to the next bin.

This works because most incoming pallets already have some natural grouping — a case here, a shrink-wrapped set there. Match that grouping to your bins instead of fighting it. If a bin is going to end up with 40 units of something, you don't need to scan all 40 individually if your system lets you log a quantity against a scan. But you do need to scan the bin and the product once, correctly, rather than trusting that you'll remember to reconcile it at the end of the day.

When to label a new bin

Most receiving hiccups aren't about the product — they're about a bin that doesn't have a label yet. If you're setting up a new shelf, a new overflow spot, or splitting a bin because it's overloaded, label it before the product goes in, not after. An unlabeled bin with product already in it is the single most common reason inventory counts drift: someone puts something away "temporarily" and it's still there three weeks later, invisible to the system.

  • New bin, new location: label first, always. It takes thirty seconds and prevents a mystery pile later.
  • Existing bin, same product: no new label needed, just scan and add to the count.
  • Existing bin, new product sharing the space: this is where people skip labeling because "it's already labeled." Rename or add to the label so it reflects what's actually in there now, or you'll open that bin in a month and have no idea why there are two SKUs in it.

If you're using Bins-USA, printing a label for a new bin and scanning it into the system takes about as long as writing it on a piece of tape by hand — except it's actually searchable later, and it ties straight into whatever pick lists or cycle counts you run afterward.

Don't let the packing slip be the only record

A packing slip tells you what was supposed to be on the pallet. It doesn't tell you where any of it ended up. If your only record of receiving is a signed slip in a folder, you've recorded the transaction but not the location — which means the next person who needs to find that product is starting from zero. The scan-as-you-unload approach solves both problems in the same motion: you're confirming the delivery matches the slip, and you're recording exactly which bin holds what, without a second pass.

This is also where shortages and overages get caught early. If a box is missing or a count is off, you'll notice it while the pallet's still in front of you and the driver's still there — not three weeks later when someone can't find the last case of something that was never actually delivered.

The afternoon you're trying not to lose

The version of receiving that eats a whole afternoon is the one where unloading, counting, and system entry happen as three separate passes, usually on three different days. The version that takes an hour is the one where they happen as one pass: unload a box, scan it into its bin, move on. It's not faster because of any special trick — it's faster because you're not doing the work twice.

title: Finding the stock that is not moving
titleEs: Encontrar la mercancía que no se está moviendo
brief: How dead stock hides in a warehouse, what 90 days of no movement really costs, and what to do about it.
briefEs: Cómo se esconde el stock muerto en una bodega, lo que de verdad cuestan 90 días sin movimiento, y qué hacer al respecto.
body:
Every warehouse has stock that just sits there. It's not damaged, not returned, not miscounted — it's just quietly taking up a shelf while nobody looks at it. The trouble is that dead stock doesn't announce itself. It looks exactly like good stock until you go check the last time it sold.

Why dead stock hides so well

Slow-moving inventory blends in because your eyes are drawn to the busy parts of the warehouse — the bins you're in and out of every day. The stuff that isn't moving is, by definition, the stuff nobody visits. You could walk past the same box for six months and never notice, because noticing it requires actively looking for absence, not presence.

It also hides in the numbers. Your total inventory value looks fine on paper. Your sell-through rate for the catalog as a whole looks fine too, because a handful of fast movers can cover for a long tail of slow ones. Dead stock is a problem that averages out of view.

What 90 days of no movement actually costs

Ninety days is a reasonable line to draw for most small retail and wholesale operations — long enough that seasonal lulls don't trip a false alarm, short enough that you catch problems before they compound. Once something crosses that line, here's what it's actually costing you, even if no line item on your P&L says so directly:

  • Space. A bin or shelf slot holding dead stock is a slot you can't use for something that would actually sell. If you're paying for square footage, that space has a cost whether it's earning or not.
  • Cash. Money spent on inventory that isn't selling is money that isn't available for inventory that would. It's tied up, not gone, but tied up cash still isn't cash you can use.
  • Labor. Every cycle count, every reorganization, every time someone has to move a shelf to get at something behind it — dead stock adds friction to tasks that have nothing to do with it.
  • Decisions. Stale inventory numbers skew your reorder decisions. If a system or a person is looking at total units on hand without accounting for what's actually selling, you risk reordering fresh stock while old stock of the same or a similar item sits untouched.

None of this is dramatic on its own. It's the kind of cost that's easy to shrug off in any given week, but it adds up across a year, and across every slow-moving SKU you're carrying without realizing it.

How to actually find it

You don't need a fancy system to start. You need a habit and a place to look.

If you're doing this manually, pull a report of last-sold dates for every SKU and sort by oldest. Anything with no sale in 90 days goes on a list. Then physically check a sample of that list against the shelf — sometimes "no sale" means the item is genuinely dead, and sometimes it means it was miscounted, mislabeled, or sitting in a bin nobody scans.

If you're using a system that tracks bin locations and movement, this gets a lot faster, because you can pull last-activity by bin instead of relying on memory or a walkthrough. This is a place where Bins-USA earns its keep — since every pick, receive, and transfer is logged against a specific bin, you can see at a glance which locations haven't been touched in months, without having to guess or walk the floor. That turns "we should probably audit this sometime" into a report you can actually run.

What to do once you've found it

Finding dead stock is only useful if you follow it with a decision. A few realistic options:

  • Discount it and move it. A markdown that clears the bin is usually better than a bin that sits full for another quarter.
  • Bundle it. Slow movers sometimes sell fine when paired with something that does move, especially if the bundle price feels like a deal.
  • Return it to the vendor. If you have a return or restocking agreement, this is often the cleanest option, even at a partial loss.
  • Write it off. Sometimes the honest answer is that the stock isn't coming back to life, and the bin space is worth more than the hope of a sale.

Whatever you choose, do it on a schedule — monthly or quarterly — rather than only when you happen to notice a full shelf that shouldn't be full.

Dead stock isn't a moral failing or a sign you bought wrong. It's a normal byproduct of running a warehouse with more than a few SKUs. The only mistake is not checking for it.

title: What your warehouse staff should not see
titleEs: Lo que su personal de bodega no debería ver
brief: Costs, margins and payouts on a shared tablet, and how to give someone the picking screen and nothing else.
briefEs: Costos, márgenes y pagos en una tablet compartida, y cómo darle a alguien la pantalla de selección y nada más.
body:
A shared tablet on the warehouse floor is convenient. Anyone can grab it, look up a pick list, mark an order shipped, and move on. But that same convenience means anyone can also grab it and see whatever the last person left open — including screens that were never meant for a warehouse floor at all.

This isn't really about trust. Most warehouse staff couldn't care less what your margin is on a case of bolts. It's about what happens when the wrong screen is one tap away, on a device that gets picked up by whoever is closest, logged into whatever account was convenient at the time.

What ends up on the shared device

It happens gradually, not on purpose. Someone logs into the full Shopify admin to check on an order. A manager pulls up a supplier invoice to answer a question, then walks away. A payout report gets left open because someone was reconciling deposits. None of this is a policy failure — it's just what happens when one tablet serves five different jobs.

The problem is that a warehouse tablet gets handled differently than an office computer. It sits on a cart. It gets passed between shifts. It doesn't lock itself after two minutes because someone is mid-scan. So whatever is open, stays open, in front of whoever walks by — including temp staff, delivery drivers waiting at the dock, or a new hire on day one.

Costs and margins are not floor information

There are good reasons to keep landed cost, wholesale pricing, and margin data off the floor, and none of them are about secrecy for its own sake:

  • Staff turnover in warehouses tends to be higher than in the office, so the fewer people who see pricing data, the smaller your exposure if someone leaves on bad terms.
  • Margin numbers create awkward conversations that have nothing to do with getting orders out the door — "why do we sell this for so much" is not a productive break-room topic.
  • If a competitor or a customer ever gets a look at that tablet, cost data is the one thing you really don't want them walking away with.

None of this requires elaborate security. It requires making sure the tool your pickers use physically cannot show them that information, rather than trusting everyone to just not look.

Payouts are worse, not just more of the same

Cost and margin data is sensitive. Payout information is a different category of problem. A screen that shows bank deposits, payout schedules, or processor fees tells anyone looking at it exactly how much money is moving and when. That's not a "please don't peek" situation — that's a "this should never render on a shared device" situation.

If your current setup means logging into the same Shopify account on the warehouse tablet that your office uses for finance, payouts are one accidental tab away from being visible to whoever picks up that tablet next. The fix isn't a sticky note reminding people to log out. The fix is giving warehouse staff a login that structurally cannot open those screens.

Give them the picking screen and nothing else

This is the actual goal: a warehouse account that opens directly to bin locations and pick lists, and has no path to anything else. Not "please don't click there" — no button that leads there in the first place.

Bins-USA handles this with separate user roles. A picker logs in and sees bin locations, pick lists, and scan-to-confirm screens — the things they need to find a product and get it out the door. They don't see cost fields, supplier pricing, or financial reports, because those aren't part of what that role can open. It's the difference between telling someone not to look in a drawer and not giving them a drawer that opens.

This also solves the shared-tablet problem directly. It doesn't matter who picks up the device on a given shift, because the account tied to that role only ever shows warehouse operations. You're not relying on people remembering to log out of the admin panel before their break. There's no admin panel to log out of.

A simple test

Hand your warehouse tablet to someone outside the company — a delivery driver, a new temp, anyone unfamiliar with your setup — and see what they can find in thirty seconds without asking a question. If the answer includes anything with a dollar figure that isn't a retail price, that's worth fixing before it's someone else's problem to discover.

Separating what the floor needs from what the office sees isn't complicated. It just needs to be built into the login, not left to good intentions.
